description:
Explorando nuevos retos y ganando experiencia.

Queremos y creemos en que nuestro proyecto pueda ayudar y mejorar la experiencia de nuestros astronautas durante su estancia en el espacio.
summary:
CREW (Companion for Resilience, Evaluation & Wellbeing) is an offline-first health companion for astronauts on long-duration missions.

It combines an interactive human body dashboard, a four-level alert system (green, yellow, orange and red), and four AI companions: the Doctor, who explains results and prepares reports; the Psychologist, who offers wellbeing support; the Professor, who teaches medical concepts and offers mini brain games to keep the mind sharp; and the Pet, which motivates healthy habits.

Space hazards like isolation, distance and closed environments, among others, affect health in combined ways. CREW compares each astronaut against their own baseline and uses an auditable, deterministic ruled engine to detect combinations of signals, such as less sleep, rising blood pressure and slower reactions. The AI only explains alerts; it never decides severity or invents diagnoses. When Earth is too far away, CREW still shows the data, the procedure to follow and a report queued for later transmission.

As missions move beyond Earth’s reach, astronauts must manage their health autonomously. CREW turns scattered data into safe, understandable action, supports mental wellbeing and protects privacy. It could also help remote settings on Earth.
details:
CREW (Companion for Resilience, Evaluation & Wellbeing) is an autonomous health monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration missions, built to keep working when Earth is close enough or far too unreachable. It runs on six connected components:

  1. Data capture: Biomedical sensors (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, activity and sleep), manual questionnaires (mood, stress, fatigue and symptoms) and cognitive tests, all validated before storage.
  2. Local database: Stores measurements, mission events and each astronaut’s personal baseline, so CREW compares the crew members against themselves while respecting all safety limits.
  3. Medical evaluation engine: Deterministic, auditable ruled validated data, analyze trends, detect combinations of signals (e.g. less sleep, more stress, slower reactions, ...) and assign a four-level alert: green, yellow, orange or red. It never diagnoses.
  4. Protocol engine: Links each alert to pre-approved, step-by-step procedures. Available offline.
  5. Interface and AI companions: An interactive 3D body, charts and four characters running on a local AI model. The Doctor explains results and prepares reports. The Psychologist offers non-clinical wellbeing support. The Professor teaches medical concepts, helps the astronauts prepare for situations such as gravity transitions, and offers mini brain games (like sudoku) to keep an active mind. The Pet motivates healthy habits and collects cognitive data through reflex, memory and attention games.
  6. Earth communication: Reports are queued and sent with delay-tolerant networking when a link exists, with urgent messages prioritized.

The AI never changes alert levels. If it fails, monitoring, alerts and protocols keep running.

What are the benefits?
Astronauts understand their own health, catch subtle changes early and know exactly what to do next, without having to wait for Earth. Doctors receive structured reports. The system supports mental wellbeing, keeps medical, psychological and gamification data separate, and protects privacy.

What is the expected impact?
CREW can make long missions to the Moon and Mars safer by turning scattered data into safe, autonomous decisions and reducing the isolation astronauts face. The same architecture could help remote areas on Earth, such as polar bases, expeditions and isolated facilities, after proper adaptation and validation.

What tools, languages, hardware and software were used?

Hardware: CREW is thought to be implemented in the NASA hardware, as a plus rather than it being a completly new machine.

Software:

  • We used HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Three.js to program the demo and shape an example of our idea.
  • We used Figma, GitHub and Visual Studio Code, with some plug-ins offered in each, to think about the architecture and to write the code.

How is it creative?

CREW combines a body-based dashboard, explainable rules, AI companions and gamification in one system. Its most original idea is the Pet: a friendly companion that builds healthy habits while quietly collecting cognitive indicators, and never punishes or guilt-trips the user. Its safety-first design, with AI strictly subordinate to the rules engine, is also distinctive.

What factors did we consider?

We have taken into consideration NASA’s five hazards of spaceflight (radiation, isolation, distance, gravity and closed environments), how they interact, communication delays, individual differences, safety and explainability, offline autonomy, privacy and mandatory safety reporting, and positive motivation.

We also stayed honest about limits: thresholds are illustrative, cognitive games are exploratory rather than clinical, and real use would require medical validation.
